title: Making Connections With Rational Functions and Equations
overview: Rational functions are the language of many scientific laws – from how loud a concert is to how deep a diver can go. In this section you will model real situations, decide whether to analyse a function or solve an equation, and handle two special cases: **holes** and **oblique asymptotes**.
objectives: Model inverse-variation and inverse-square situations and solve related problems.
Decide whether a problem requires analysing a function or solving an equation or inequality.
Identify holes and find their coordinates.
Find oblique asymptotes using long division.
Interpret rates of change and average values in context.
Carry out a full numeric, algebraic, graphical and verbal analysis.

lessons.title: Inverse variation and the inverse square law
lessons.body:
Many laws of science are rational functions.

| Relationship | Formula | Example |
|---|---|---|
| inverse variation | $y = \dfrac{k}{x}$ | Boyle's law: gas volume $V = \frac{k}{P}$ at constant temperature |
| inverse square | $y = \dfrac{k}{x^2}$ | sound or light intensity $I = \frac{k}{d^2}$; gravity |
| joint variation | $y = \dfrac{kx}{z^2}$ | wire resistance $R = \frac{kl}{d^2}$ |

**Finding $k$:** substitute one known pair of values.

**Example – sound.** The intensity of sound from a speaker is 0.001 W/m² at 2 m. Then $0.001 = \frac{k}{2^2}$, so $k = 0.004$ and $I = \dfrac{0.004}{d^2}$, $d > 0$.

**Halving the distance:** $I\left(\frac{d}{2}\right) = \dfrac{0.004}{d^2/4} = 4 \times \dfrac{0.004}{d^2}$ – the sound is **four times** as intense. This is why moving closer at a concert is so much louder.

```plot
title: I = 0.004/d² (W/m²) against distance d (m)
f: 0.004/x^2
domain: 0, 8
range: 0, 0.005
points: (2,0.001)
ticks: 1, 0.001
```

lessons.title: Modelling and solving: read the question carefully
lessons.body:
In a problem, first decide whether you are asked to **analyse a function** (describe features, sketch, rates of change) or to **solve an equation or inequality** (find values).

**Example – diving.** The maximum time $T$ (min) a scuba diver can stay at depth $d$ (m) and rise without decompression stops is $T(d) = \dfrac{525}{d - 10}$, $d > 10$. For what depths is this time less than 30 min?

$$\frac{525}{d - 10} < 30$$

Because $d > 10$, the denominator is positive, so there is only **one case** and we may multiply without flipping:

$525 < 30(d - 10) \Rightarrow 17.5 < d - 10 \Rightarrow d > 27.5$

Deeper than 27.5 m, the no-stop time is under 30 min.

```plot
title: T(d) = 525/(d − 10)
f: 525/(x-10)
f: 30 | dashed
domain: 10, 90
range: 0, 100
points: (27.5,30)
asymptote x: 10
ticks: 10, 10
```

lessons.title: Special case 1: holes
lessons.body:
If the numerator and denominator share a factor, the function **simplifies** – but the original restriction remains.

$$f(x) = \frac{x^2 + x - 6}{x - 2} = \frac{(x + 3)(x - 2)}{x - 2} = x + 3, \quad x \ne 2$$

The graph is the line $y = x + 3$ with a **hole** at $(2, 5)$: as $x \to 2$, $f(x) \to 5$, but $f(2)$ is undefined. A hole is a **discontinuity that is not an asymptote**.

```plot
title: f(x) = (x² + x − 6)/(x − 2): a line with a hole at (2, 5)
f: (x^2+x-6)/(x-2)
domain: -6, 6
range: -4, 9
points: (2,5)
```

A function can have both: $g(x) = \dfrac{2x^2 + 7x - 4}{2x^2 - 5x + 2} = \dfrac{(2x - 1)(x + 4)}{(2x - 1)(x - 2)} = \dfrac{x + 4}{x - 2}$, $x \ne \frac{1}{2}$, has a vertical asymptote $x = 2$, a horizontal asymptote $y = 1$, **and** a hole at $\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{4.5}{-1.5}\right) = \left(\frac{1}{2}, -3\right)$.

> To find the hole's $y$-coordinate, substitute the cancelled $x$-value into the **simplified** function.

lessons.title: Special case 2: oblique (slant) asymptotes
lessons.body:
When the degree of the numerator is **one more** than the degree of the denominator, the graph has an **oblique (slant) asymptote** – a line that is neither horizontal nor vertical.

Use **long division** to rewrite the function:

$$f(x) = \frac{x^2 + 2x + 5}{x + 1} = x + 1 + \frac{4}{x + 1}$$

As $x \to \pm\infty$, $\frac{4}{x + 1} \to 0$, so the graph approaches the line $y = x + 1$. There is still a vertical asymptote $x = -1$.

```plot
title: Oblique asymptote y = x + 1
f: (x^2+2*x+5)/(x+1)
f: x+1 | dashed; label=y = x + 1
domain: -8, 6
range: -12, 12
asymptote x: -1
```

**Summary of asymptote rules for $\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$** (after cancelling common factors):
* degree $P$ < degree $Q$: horizontal asymptote $y = 0$;
* degree $P$ = degree $Q$: horizontal asymptote $y = $ ratio of leading coefficients;
* degree $P$ = degree $Q$ + 1: oblique asymptote = the quotient from division.

lessons.title: Rates of change in context
lessons.body:
Rates of change answer "how fast is it changing?" questions.

* **Average rate of change** over an interval = slope of the secant: $\dfrac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$.
* **Instantaneous rate** at a point ≈ slope of a secant over a very small interval.
* **Average value per unit**, such as average profit per kilogram $\frac{P(x)}{x}$, is the slope of the secant from the **origin** to $(x, P(x))$.

**Example – fertilizer profit.** $P(x) = \dfrac{600x - 15\,000}{x + 100}$ (thousands of dollars, $x$ in tonnes).
* Break-even: $P(x) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 25$ t.
* Long run: horizontal asymptote $P = 600$ – profit levels off at 600 thousand dollars.
* Rate at $x = 100$: $\frac{P(100.01) - P(100)}{0.01} \approx 1.875$ thousand dollars per tonne; at $x = 500$ it is only about 0.208. Extra sales add less and less profit.

### A full analysis has four components
**numeric** (tables, calculations), **algebraic** (formulas, solving), **graphical** and **verbal** (describing what it means in context).

keyTerms.definition: A point discontinuity that appears when a factor cancels from the numerator and denominator.
A value of x where a function is not continuous: a vertical asymptote or a hole.
A non-horizontal, non-vertical line that the graph approaches as x → ±∞; it occurs when the numerator's degree is one more than the denominator's.
In the rocket model, the velocity at the vertical asymptote, where the maximum height becomes unbounded.
The slope of a secant line between two points of a function.

formulas.name: Inverse variation
formulas.meaning: Find k from one data point.

formulas.name: Oblique asymptote by division
formulas.meaning: When deg P = deg Q + 1, the linear quotient is the slant asymptote.

workedExamples.title: Intensity of sound
workedExamples.problem: Sound intensity varies inversely as the square of the distance. It is 0.001 W/m² at 2 m. (a) Find the equation. (b) What happens when you halve the distance?
workedExamples.answer: $I = \dfrac{0.004}{d^2}$; halving the distance makes the sound 4 times as intense.

workedExamples.title: Special cases
workedExamples.problem: Sketch $g(x) = \dfrac{2x^2 + 7x - 4}{2x^2 - 5x + 2}$ and explain why it is a special case.
workedExamples.answer: A linear-over-linear graph with an extra hole at $(\frac{1}{2}, -3)$.

workedExamples.title: Oblique asymptote
steps: Vertical asymptote $x = 3$; oblique asymptote $y = x - 2$; no horizontal asymptote.

workedExamples.title: Parallel resistance
workedExamples.problem: A resistor of $x$ Ω in parallel with a 1 Ω resistor gives $R(x) = \dfrac{x}{x + 1}$. For what $x$ is $R < 0.25$ Ω?

misconceptions.myth: $\dfrac{x^2 + x - 6}{x - 2}$ has a vertical asymptote at $x = 2$.
misconceptions.fact: The factor $(x - 2)$ cancels, so there is a **hole** at $(2, 5)$, not an asymptote.

misconceptions.myth: A rational function always has a horizontal asymptote.
misconceptions.fact: If the numerator's degree is one more than the denominator's, the graph has an **oblique** asymptote instead.

misconceptions.myth: Halving the distance doubles the intensity.
misconceptions.fact: In an inverse square law it **quadruples** the intensity.

misconceptions.myth: A model is valid for every real number.
misconceptions.fact: Context restricts the domain: distances, times and amounts are usually positive, so only part of the graph applies.

misconceptions.myth: The hole's $y$-coordinate is found by substituting into the original function.
misconceptions.fact: The original is undefined there; substitute into the **simplified** function.

realWorld.title: Concert safety
realWorld.body: Inverse-square sound laws are used to set safe distances from speakers; standing twice as close means four times the intensity.

realWorld.title: Space travel
realWorld.body: In the model $h = \frac{6400v^2}{125\,440 - v^2}$, the vertical asymptote at $v = \sqrt{125\,440} \approx 354$ is the escape velocity: the speed at which the rocket never comes back down.

realWorld.title: Electronics
realWorld.body: Resistors in parallel combine as $\frac{R_1R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$, a rational function that engineers solve to hit a target resistance.

realWorld.title: Food safety
realWorld.body: A freezer's temperature after a power failure, $T = \frac{2t^2}{t + 1} - 15$, tells a plant manager how long food stays frozen – a model with an oblique asymptote.

realWorld.title: Medicine
realWorld.body: Drug concentration models like $C(t) = \frac{0.16t}{t^2 + t + 2}$ rise to a peak and then decay toward 0 as the drug leaves the bloodstream.

practice.question: Light intensity is 6 lux at 50 m. Write the inverse-square model and find the intensity at 10 m.
A tank holds 10 L of gas at 500 kPa. Using Boyle's law $V = \frac{k}{P}$, find the volume at 800 kPa.
Find the oblique asymptote of $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 + 3x + 1}{x + 1}$.
practice.solution: $x^2 + 3x + 1 = (x + 1)(x + 2) - 1$, so the slant asymptote is $y = x + 2$.

practice.question: A cylindrical tank has volume 100 000 cm³. Write $h$ in terms of $r$.
For $x > 0$, what value of $x$ gives the least value of $x + \frac{1}{x}$?
practice.solution: $x = 1$ gives 2; values on either side are larger (0.5 → 2.5, 2 → 2.5).

summary: Inverse variation $y = \frac{k}{x}$ and inverse-square laws $y = \frac{k}{x^2}$ model many physical situations; find $k$ from known data.
Decide whether a problem asks you to analyse a function or to solve an equation or inequality.
Common factors cause **holes**; find their $y$-values from the simplified function.
When the numerator's degree is one more than the denominator's, long division gives an **oblique asymptote**.
Rates of change in context come from secant slopes; average value per unit is the slope of a secant from the origin.
A full analysis is numeric, algebraic, graphical and verbal.

questions.text: The intensity of sound varies inversely as the square of the distance from the source. At {{d0}} m from a speaker the intensity is {{I0}} W/m².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the intensity at {{d1}} m.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What is the effect of halving the distance? Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $I = \dfrac{k}{d^2}$; $k = {{I0}} \times {{d0}}^2 = {{I0*d0^2:4}}$. So $I = \dfrac{ {{I0*d0^2:4}} }{d^2}$, $d > 0$.

(b) $I({{d1}}) = \dfrac{ {{I0*d0^2:4}} }{ {{d1^2}} } \approx {{I0*d0^2/d1^2:3}}$ W/m².

(c) Halving the distance: $\dfrac{k}{(d/2)^2} = \dfrac{4k}{d^2}$ – four times as intense.

rubric.point: Halving distance ⇒ 4 times with algebraic reason

questions.text: According to Boyle's law, at constant temperature the volume of a gas varies inversely with pressure. A tank holds {{V0}} L of hydrogen at {{P0}} kPa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the volume at {{P1}} kPa.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What is the effect of doubling the pressure?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the graph.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $V = \dfrac{k}{P}$, $k = {{V0}} \times {{P0}} = {{V0*P0}}$: $V = \dfrac{ {{V0*P0}} }{P}$, $P > 0$.

(b) $V({{P1}}) = \dfrac{ {{V0*P0}} }{ {{P1}} } \approx {{V0*P0/P1:3}}$ L.

(c) Doubling the pressure halves the volume, because $PV$ is constant.

(d) The graph is the first-quadrant branch of a reciprocal function: decreasing, approaching $V = 0$ as $P$ grows and growing without bound as $P \to 0^+$.

questions.text: A resistor of $x$ ohms connected in parallel with a 1 Ω resistor gives a total resistance of $R(x) = \dfrac{x}{x + 1}$ ohms, $x > 0$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find $x$ for a total resistance of {{r}} Ω.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For what $x$ is the total resistance less than {{r}} Ω?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Interpret the horizontal asymptote.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\dfrac{x}{x + 1} = {{r}}$: $x = {{r}}x + {{r}}$, so ${{1-r}}x = {{r}}$ and $x = \dfrac{ {{r}} }{ {{1-r}} } \approx {{r/(1-r):3}}$ Ω.

(b) Since $x > 0$, $x + 1 > 0$, so $\dfrac{x}{x+1} < {{r}} \Rightarrow x < {{r}}(x + 1) \Rightarrow {{1-r}}x < {{r}} \Rightarrow x < {{r/(1-r):3}}$. Solution: $0 < x < {{r/(1-r):3}}$ Ω.

(c) Horizontal asymptote $R = 1$: however large $x$ is, the total resistance is always less than 1 Ω (the smaller resistor).

questions.text: The maximum time $T$, in minutes, a scuba diver can stay at depth $d$ metres and rise without decompression stops is $T(d) = \dfrac{525}{d - 10}$, $d > 10$. For the maximum time to be less than {{T0}} min, how deep must the diver be?

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the boundary depth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your solution.

questions.modelAnswer:
Solve $\dfrac{525}{d - 10} < {{T0}}$. Because $d > 10$, $d - 10 > 0$: only one case, multiply without flipping.

$525 < {{T0}}(d - 10) \Rightarrow d - 10 > \dfrac{525}{ {{T0}} } \approx {{525/T0:4}} \Rightarrow d > {{10+525/T0:4}}$.

At depths greater than about {{10+525/T0:3}} m the no-stop time is under {{T0}} min. Graphically, this is where the curve lies below the line $T = {{T0}}$.

rubric.point: Justifies a single case using d > 10

questions.text: Sketch (by describing) the graph of $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 + {{a-b}}x - {{a*b}}}{x - {{b}}}$ and explain why it is a special case.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the $y$-coordinate of the hole.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the graph and explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
Factor the numerator: $x^2 + ({{a}} - {{b}})x - {{a*b}} = (x + {{a}})(x - {{b}})$.

So $f(x) = \dfrac{(x + {{a}})(x - {{b}})}{x - {{b}}} = x + {{a}}$, $x \ne {{b}}$.

The graph is the line $y = x + {{a}}$ (slope 1, $y$-intercept {{a}}, $x$-intercept $-{{a}}$) with a **hole** at $({{b}}, {{a+b}})$. It is a special case because the zero of the denominator does not produce a vertical asymptote – the common factor cancels, leaving a discontinuity that is a single missing point.

rubric.point: Explains why it is a special case

questions.text: Analyse $g(x) = \dfrac{2x^2 + 7x - 4}{2x^2 - 5x + 2}$: find all asymptotes, intercepts and any holes, and describe the graph.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Vertical asymptote $x = ?$

parts.label: b
parts.text: $y$-coordinate of the hole.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Complete the analysis.

questions.modelAnswer:
Factor: $g(x) = \dfrac{(2x - 1)(x + 4)}{(2x - 1)(x - 2)}$. Restrictions $x \ne \frac{1}{2}$, $x \ne 2$.

Simplified: $g(x) = \dfrac{x + 4}{x - 2}$, $x \ne \frac{1}{2}$.

* Vertical asymptote $x = 2$ (the factor $x - 2$ does not cancel).
* Horizontal asymptote $y = 1$.
* $x$-intercept $-4$; $y$-intercept $g(0) = -2$.
* Hole: $\frac{0.5 + 4}{0.5 - 2} = -3$, so a hole at $(0.5, -3)$.

The graph is the linear-over-linear curve $y = \frac{x + 4}{x - 2}$ (decreasing on both branches) with one point removed at $(0.5, -3)$ on its left branch.

questions.text: The function $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 + {{b}}x + {{c}}}{x + 1}$ has an oblique asymptote. Use long division to find it, and state the vertical asymptote.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The oblique asymptote is $y = x + k$. Find $k$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show the division and state the vertical asymptote.

questions.modelAnswer:
Divide $x^2 + {{b}}x + {{c}}$ by $x + 1$:

$x^2 + {{b}}x + {{c}} = (x + 1)(x + {{b-1}}) + {{c-b+1}}$.

So $f(x) = x + {{b-1}} + \dfrac{ {{c-b+1}} }{x + 1}$.

As $x \to \pm\infty$, $\dfrac{ {{c-b+1}} }{x + 1} \to 0$, so the oblique asymptote is $y = x + {{b-1}}$. The vertical asymptote is $x = -1$ (the remainder {{c-b+1}} is not zero, so nothing cancels).

questions.text: After a power failure, the temperature in a freezer is modelled by $T(t) = \dfrac{2t^2}{t + 1} - 15$, where $T$ is in °C and $t$ is in hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How long until the temperature reaches 0 °C?

parts.label: b
parts.text: A generator starts at −5 °C. When does this happen?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the long-run behaviour of the model.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Set $T = 0$: $\dfrac{2t^2}{t + 1} = 15 \Rightarrow 2t^2 = 15t + 15 \Rightarrow 2t^2 - 15t - 15 = 0$.

$t = \dfrac{15 + \sqrt{225 + 120}}{4} = \dfrac{15 + \sqrt{345}}{4} \approx 8.39$ h (the negative root is rejected).

(b) Set $T = -5$: $\dfrac{2t^2}{t + 1} = 10 \Rightarrow t^2 - 5t - 5 = 0 \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{5 + \sqrt{45}}{2} \approx 5.85$ h.

(c) Dividing, $\frac{2t^2}{t+1} = 2t - 2 + \frac{2}{t + 1}$, so $T \approx 2t - 17$ for large $t$: an oblique asymptote. In reality the temperature would level off at room temperature, so the model is only reasonable for the first several hours.

rubric.point: Comments on long-run behaviour/limits of the model

questions.text: A cylindrical tank is to have a volume of {{V}} cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write $h$ in terms of $r$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the height when the radius is {{r1}} cm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the radius when the height is {{h1}} cm.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the graph.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $V = \pi r^2 h$, so $h = \dfrac{ {{V}} }{\pi r^2}$, $r > 0$.

(b) $h({{r1}}) = \dfrac{ {{V}} }{\pi ({{r1}})^2} \approx {{V/(pi*r1^2):3}}$ cm.

(c) $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{ {{V}} }{\pi ({{h1}})}} \approx {{sqrt(V/(pi*h1)):3}}$ cm.

(d) The graph is a decreasing curve in the first quadrant: as $r \to 0^+$, $h$ grows without bound (vertical asymptote $r = 0$); as $r$ increases, $h \to 0$ (horizontal asymptote $h = 0$). It is an inverse-square relationship.

questions.text: A bus company models its cost per person for a charter trip by $C(x) = \dfrac{10\,000}{10 + x}$ dollars, where $x$ is the number of passengers over its minimum of 10. Describe how each change alters the model and its graph: (a) $C(x) = \dfrac{10\,000}{8 + x}$ (b) $C(x) = \dfrac{20\,000}{10 + x}$ (c) $C(x) = \dfrac{15\,000}{12 + x}$. Also find the cost per person in the original model when $x = {{x1}}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cost per person in the original model when $x = {{x1}}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe each change.

questions.modelAnswer:
Original: $C({{x1}}) = \dfrac{10\,000}{ {{10+x1}} } \approx {{10000/(10+x1):4}}$ dollars per person. (Total cost 10 000 dollars shared among $10 + x$ people.)

(a) Vertical asymptote moves from $x = -10$ to $x = -8$: the minimum group is now 8, and the graph shifts 2 units right; at $x = 0$ each person pays 1250 instead of 1000.

(b) Vertical stretch by a factor of 2: the total charter cost doubles to 20 000 dollars, so every per-person cost doubles.

(c) Total cost 15 000 dollars and a minimum of 12 people: stretched by 1.5 and shifted 2 units left; $C(0) = 1250$.

In all cases the horizontal asymptote is $C = 0$: with more passengers the per-person cost keeps falling toward 0.

questions.text: The electric power $P$, in watts, delivered by a battery is $P = \dfrac{100R}{(2 + R)^2}$, where $R$ is the resistance in ohms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the power when $R = 2$ Ω.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the rate of change is 0 at $R = 2$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What does this indicate? Describe the power as $R$ increases from 0 to 20 Ω.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $P(2) = \dfrac{200}{16} = 12.5$ W.

(b) Secant from $R = 1.99$ to $R = 2.01$: $P(1.99) = \dfrac{199}{15.9201} \approx 12.49992$ and $P(2.01) = \dfrac{201}{16.0801} \approx 12.49992$, so the slope $\approx \dfrac{0}{0.02} = 0$. The rate of change is 0 at $R = 2$.

(c) Rate 0 at the top of the curve means the power is at its **maximum**, 12.5 W, when $R = 2$ Ω. For $0 < R < 2$ the power increases; for $R > 2$ it decreases toward 0 (horizontal asymptote $P = 0$, since the denominator has the higher degree).

rubric.point: Describes behaviour from 0 to 20 Ω with asymptote

questions.text: The acceleration due to gravity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the centre of Earth. For a satellite 7000 km from the centre of Earth it is 8.2 m/s².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the formula.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At what distance from Earth's centre is the acceleration {{a1}} m/s²?

parts.label: c
parts.text: How high above the surface is that (Earth's radius is 6400 km)?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $g = \dfrac{k}{d^2}$; $k = 8.2 \times 7000^2 = 4.018 \times 10^8$. So $g = \dfrac{4.018 \times 10^8}{d^2}$.

(b) $d = \sqrt{\dfrac{4.018 \times 10^8}{ {{a1}} }} \approx {{sqrt(8.2*7000^2/a1):4}}$ km from the centre.

(c) Above the surface (radius 6400 km): about {{sqrt(8.2*7000^2/a1)-6400:3}} km.

questions.text: A manufacturer predicts profit $P$, in thousands of dollars, from selling $x$ tonnes of fertilizer: $P(x) = \dfrac{600x - 15\,000}{x + 100}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Break-even sales.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the predicted profit as sales increase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Estimate the rate of change of profit at 100 t.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Estimate the rate at 500 t and compare.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $P(x) = 0 \Rightarrow 600x = 15\,000 \Rightarrow x = 25$ t (break-even).

(b) Horizontal asymptote $P = 600$: profit approaches 600 thousand dollars as sales grow, but never exceeds it.

(c) Secant estimates: at 100 t, $\frac{P(100.01) - P(100)}{0.01} \approx 1.875$; at 500 t, $\approx 0.208$ (thousand dollars per tonne). Profit grows much more slowly at higher sales.

questions.text: The maximum height $h$, in kilometres, of a rocket launched with initial velocity $v$ is $h = \dfrac{6400v^2}{125\,440 - v^2}$, ignoring air resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the maximum height for $v = {{v1}}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the velocity at the vertical asymptote is the escape velocity.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $h({{v1}}) = \dfrac{6400({{v1}})^2}{125\,440 - {{v1^2}} } \approx {{6400*v1^2/(125440-v1^2):3}}$ km.

(b) The vertical asymptote is where $125\,440 - v^2 = 0$: $v = \sqrt{125\,440} \approx 354.2$. As $v$ approaches this value from below, the maximum height grows without bound – the rocket never falls back. That is the meaning of escape velocity: the speed needed to break free of Earth's gravity. For speeds above it the formula gives negative heights, which have no meaning.

rubric.point: Comments on the domain beyond the asymptote

questions.text: For the profit model $P(x) = \dfrac{600x - 15\,000}{x + 100}$ (thousands of dollars, $x$ tonnes), the average profit per tonne at sales level $x$ is $\dfrac{P(x)}{x}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the connection to secants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the average profit per tonne at {{x1}} t.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Where is the average profit greatest? Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The secant from the origin $(0, 0)$ to $(x, P(x))$ has slope $\frac{P(x) - 0}{x - 0} = \frac{P(x)}{x}$ – the average profit per tonne.

(b) At $x = {{x1}}$: $\dfrac{P({{x1}})}{ {{x1}} } \approx \dfrac{ {{(600*x1-15000)/(x1+100):4}} }{ {{x1}} } \approx {{(600*x1-15000)/(x1+100)/x1:3}}$ thousand dollars per tonne.

(c) The average profit is greatest where the secant from the origin is steepest, i.e. where it just touches the curve (is tangent to it). A table of $\frac{P(x)}{x}$ shows the largest value near $x \approx 81$ t (about 2.29 thousand dollars per tonne).

rubric.point: Explains secant slope as average profit
Explains where the maximum occurs (tangent from origin)

questions.text: The concentration of a drug in the bloodstream is $C(t) = \dfrac{0.16t}{t^2 + t + 2}$ mg/cm³, $t$ in minutes. Give a full analysis: numeric, algebraic, graphical and verbal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the time of maximum concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the full analysis.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Algebraic:** $t^2 + t + 2$ has discriminant $1 - 8 < 0$, so no vertical asymptotes. Degree of the denominator > degree of the numerator, so horizontal asymptote $C = 0$. $C(0) = 0$.

**Numeric:** $C(1) = 0.04$, $C(1.4) \approx 0.0418$, $C(1.5) \approx 0.0417$, $C(2) = 0.04$, $C(5) \approx 0.025$, $C(20) \approx 0.0075$. The maximum is about 0.042 mg/cm³ near $t \approx 1.4$ min.

**Graphical:** starts at the origin, rises quickly to a peak at about $(1.4, 0.042)$, then decreases gradually toward 0.

**Verbal:** the drug enters the bloodstream and the concentration peaks after about 1.4 minutes; afterwards the body removes it, and the concentration approaches 0 but the model never reaches exactly 0.

questions.text: Other than at vertical asymptotes, describe when a discontinuity can occur in a rational function. Give an example and explain how to find the exact location of the discontinuity.
questions.modelAnswer:
A discontinuity also occurs where the numerator and denominator share a factor that cancels: the function is undefined there, but its values approach a finite number, giving a **hole**.

Example: $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3} = x + 3$, $x \ne 3$. To locate the hole, factor, cancel, and substitute the excluded value into the simplified expression: $3 + 3 = 6$, so the hole is at $(3, 6)$.

rubric.point: Explains how to find the hole's coordinates

questions.text: The electrical resistance $R$ (Ω) of a wire varies directly with its length $l$ (m) and inversely with the square of its diameter $d$ (mm): $R = \dfrac{kl}{d^2}$. A {{L0}} m wire of diameter {{d0}} mm has resistance {{R0}} Ω.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the resistance of {{L0}} m of {{d1}}-mm wire.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the graph of resistance against diameter.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) ${{R0}} = \dfrac{k({{L0}})}{ {{d0}}^2}$, so $k = \dfrac{ {{R0}} \times {{d0^2}} }{ {{L0}} } = {{R0*d0^2/L0:4}}$. $R = \dfrac{ {{R0*d0^2/L0:4}}\,l}{d^2}$.

(b) For $l = {{L0}}$: $R = \dfrac{ {{R0*d0^2}} }{d^2}$. At $d = {{d1}}$ mm: $R \approx {{R0*d0^2/d1^2:3}}$ Ω.

(c) The graph of $R$ against $d$ for fixed length is a decreasing inverse-square curve: thicker wire, much less resistance.

questions.text: For $x > 0$, what value of $x$ gives the least sum of $x$ and its reciprocal? Justify numerically and explain using the graph of $y = x + \dfrac{1}{x}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Value of $x$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Least sum.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Justify.

questions.modelAnswer:
Table: $x = 0.5 \to 2.5$; $0.8 \to 2.05$; $1 \to 2$; $1.25 \to 2.05$; $2 \to 2.5$. The least value is 2 at $x = 1$.

Algebraic support: $x + \frac{1}{x} - 2 = \frac{x^2 - 2x + 1}{x} = \frac{(x - 1)^2}{x} \ge 0$ for $x > 0$, with equality only at $x = 1$.

Graph: vertical asymptote $x = 0$ and oblique asymptote $y = x$; the right branch comes down from $+\infty$, reaches a minimum $(1, 2)$, then rises along the slant asymptote.

questions.text: The intensity of illumination from a light source is $I = \dfrac{k}{d^2}$ lux. At {{d0}} m the intensity is {{I0}} lux.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the model.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At what distance is the intensity {{I1}} lux?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the behaviour for large $d$ and comment on the model near $d = 0$.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $k = {{I0}} \times {{d0^2}} = {{I0*d0^2}}$, so $I = \dfrac{ {{I0*d0^2}} }{d^2}$.

(b) $d = \sqrt{\dfrac{ {{I0*d0^2}} }{ {{I1}} }} \approx {{sqrt(I0*d0^2/I1):3}}$ m.

(c) As $d$ increases the intensity decreases toward 0 (but never reaches it). For $d$ close to 0 the model gives enormous intensities, which is unrealistic – a real light source has a size, so the model only applies at distances that are large compared with the source.

rubric.point: Comments on the model near d = 0
